soil-bio-208.title: How microbes make a living, from fermenting to eating methane
soil-bio-208.text: A microbe's metabolism largely decides its ecological niche, and it can make the microbe responsible for whole cycles of elements through soil and air. Microbial metabolism is the means by which a microbe obtains the energy and nutrients, such as carbon, that it needs to live and reproduce. Following {{ref:soil-bio-207}}, metabolisms are sorted three ways. By carbon source they are autotrophic, heterotrophic or mixotrophic. By source of reducing equivalents, the electrons they use, they are lithotrophic or organotrophic. By energy source they are phototrophic or chemotrophic. Nitrifying, sulfur-oxidizing and iron-oxidizing bacteria are chemolithoautotrophs. Most bacteria, Bacillus and the Actinomycetota among them, are chemoorganoheterotrophs. Oxygen is not always on hand. Fermenters use organic carbon instead of oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor. Facultative anaerobes respire with oxygen when it is present and switch to fermentation when it is not. Many of them also denitrify, because nitrate, like oxygen, has a high reduction potential, a strong pull on electrons. They reduce nitrate step by step through nitrite, nitric oxide and nitrous oxide to dinitrogen, a form of {{ref:soil-chem-128}}. {{ref:soil-env-280}} oxidize methane step by step to carbon dioxide. The process needs oxygen, so all conventional ones are obligate aerobes. Ammonia and nitrite oxidation yield so little energy that nitrifiers grow very slowly. In 2015 one genus, {{ref:soil-fert-221}}, was shown to carry out both oxidation steps on its own, a process called {{ref:soil-fert-110}}.

soil-bio-209.title: Microarthropods, tiny animals that travel by pore
soil-bio-209.text: A microarthropod can move only through pores that already exist in the soil. These small arthropods, usually one to several millimeters long, live mostly in soil. They include springtails, mites such as Oribatida and Mesostigmata, small centipedes, small insects and their larvae, and small crustaceans. They are most common in fallen leaves, litter and the upper soil layers. There they speed the decomposition of organic matter and help form soil structure. They are very sensitive to changes in ecosystems, so their communities serve as bioindicators for environmental assessment.

soil-bio-210.title: Soil mites, eight-legged recyclers of leaf litter
soil-bio-210.text: Leaf litter teems with mites, small eight-legged arachnids, and many species live in soil as decomposers. They inhabit organic debris of all kinds. Soil mites span a range of taxa. Oribatida and Prostigmata are more numerous in soil than Mesostigmata and have more soil-dwelling species. After a disturbance such as agriculture, most mites recolonize soil within a few months, but Oribatida take several years. Most are beneficial, helping decompose organic material as part of the cycling of carbon. Some Laelapidae are even used to control fungus gnats and soil pests.

soil-bio-215.title: Nematophagous fungi, the soil's worm hunters
soil-bio-215.text: More than 700 species of fungi hunt nematodes. These nematophagous fungi are carnivores specialized in trapping and digesting the worms. Some catch prey with adhesive hyphae, knobs or nets, others with hyphal loops that tighten on contact. Still others stun nematodes with toxins or infect them or their eggs as parasites. Trappers concentrate in the upper soil, pastures and leaf litter, mostly in nitrogen-deficient habitats. Arthrobotrys oligospora builds its costly snares only when it detects nematode pheromones such as ascarosides. Purpureocillium lilacinum, which attacks the root-knot nematode Meloidogyne incognita, is studied for biological control, though field results have been mixed.

soil-bio-222.title: Counting the living with membrane fats
soil-bio-222.text: Phospholipids, the fats of cell membranes, break down rapidly when an organism dies. So the phospholipid in a soil sample is taken to come from living cells. Phospholipid fatty acid analysis, or PLFA, uses their fatty acids as chemical markers to estimate the living mass and make-up of microbial communities in soil and water. A 1965 article proposed using molecules made by organisms as biomarkers, and D.C. White pioneered the method in the early to mid 1980s. Lipids are extracted from dried soil with a chloroform–methanol–phosphate buffer. Saponifying the phospholipids releases their fatty acids. These are analyzed as methyl esters by {{ref:soil-meth-029}} and compared with those of known organisms. The method spread because it measures the dominant microbes sensitively and reproducibly, without cultivation, which is costly and biased. It has limits. The same fatty acids occur in plant roots, fungi and bacteria, so assigning them to microbial groups needs care. Archaeal lipids are ether-linked rather than ester-linked, so routine preparation misses archaea. Extraction is cumbersome, though a 96-well plate procedure raised throughput 4-to-5 fold.

soil-bio-223.title: Fatty-acid fingerprints of bacteria and fungi
soil-bio-223.text: In a flooded rice paddy, fatty acids showed archaea rising from 24% to 37% of the microbes. Such readings rest on signature fatty acids in a PLFA profile that point to particular groups. Iso- and anteiso-branched acids such as 15:0 iso estimate Gram-positive bacteria, and a methyl branch at the 10th carbon marks actinomycetes. Monounsaturated plus cyclopropane acids estimate Gram-negative bacteria; a high cyclopropane-to-monounsaturated ratio signals stress. Linoleic acid, 18:2 ω6c, indicates fungi, and 16:1 ω5c is recommended for the fungi of {{ref:soil-bio-166}}. In that paddy, aerobic bacteria fell from about 44% to 27% under longer flooding, while facultative anaerobes rose from 32% to 36%.

soil-bio-220.title: Is every microbe everywhere? Mapping microbial life
soil-bio-220.text: In 1934 Lourens Baas Becking concluded that "everything is everywhere, but the environment selects." Microbial biogeography puts that idea to the test. It studies where microorganisms live, at what abundance and why, across space and time. The field grew as cheaper, higher-throughput DNA sequencing allowed global analyses. Clear geographic patterns in microbial life now dispute Baas Becking's view. Unlike most larger organisms, global topsoil microbiomes are more diverse in temperate zones than in the tropics. Soil bacterial patterns usually track soil pH, which may stand in for the climatic water balance that controls carbon inputs and how well water-filled habitats connect.

soil-bio-245.title: Plant hormones, the tiny signals that steer roots
soil-bio-245.text: When a growing root hits an obstacle underground, its ethylene production surges and cell elongation halts. Ethylene is one of the plant hormones, signal molecules made within plants in extremely low concentrations that control growth and development. Every plant cell can make them. They are not nutrients but chemicals that, in small amounts, steer how cells grow and differentiate. Auxins promote root initiation and the growth of side roots and adventitious roots. Synthetic auxins such as IBA and NAA are sold as rooting powders for cuttings. When roots run short of water, a signal triggers the formation of ABA. Roots release it to the leaves, where it closes the stomata. {{ref:soil-bio-172}}, exuded into soil, promote the growth of the symbiotic fungi of {{ref:soil-bio-166}}. Fungi and bacteria make very similar chemicals that also affect plant growth, though in microbes they act as secondary metabolites. Went and Thimann coined the term phytohormone in their 1937 book.

soil-bio-251.title: Mutualism, the partnerships where both sides win
soil-bio-251.text: About 80% of land plant species rely on fungi for inorganic compounds and trace elements, through {{ref:soil-bio-157}}. The plants pay in carbohydrates, a "biological barter." This is mutualism, an interaction between two or more species in which each gains a net benefit. Partnerships with these fungi are linked to the colonization of land by plants. {{ref:soil-bio-178}} fix nitrogen for legumes in return for carbohydrates. In Three Sisters farming, beans fix nitrogen in the soil for the corn they climb. Mutualism can also unravel. Plant lineages in nutrient-rich places have abandoned their fungal partners many times, and those fungi can turn parasitic on weak or dying plants.

soil-bio-239.title: Rhizobium, the nitrogen fixer inside legume roots
soil-bio-239.text: In 1888 {{ref:soil-hist-016}} isolated a microbe from legume nodules and named it Bacillus radicicola; it is now placed in Rhizobium. This genus of aerobic, rod-shaped, nitrogen-fixing soil bacteria lives in root nodules, mainly of legumes. Inside, the bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia with an enzyme, {{ref:soil-fert-101}}. They pass it to the plant as glutamine or ureides and receive photosynthate, the products of photosynthesis, in return. Rhizobium can also solubilize phosphate. Not every member helps: Rhizobium rhizogenes causes hairy root disease by injecting root-inducing T-DNA into plants.

soil-bio-250.title: Plant–soil feedback: how plants shape the soil that judges their offspring
soil-bio-250.text: A plant leaves its mark on the soil, and the next plant to grow there feels it. In plant–soil feedback, plants change the biological and physical qualities of their soil, which then changes how well plants can grow in it later. Feedback is negative when a species grows worse in soil previously occupied by its own kind, and positive when it grows better. On average it tends to be negative, with many exceptions, such as many invasive species. Negative feedback was once blamed on the soil running out of nutrients. Recent work points mainly to a build-up of soil-borne pathogens, with mutualists and allelopathy also involved. That build-up helps species coexist. Abundant plants accumulate their pathogens, while rare plants escape them. Negative plant–soil feedback has been called a particular case of the Janzen–Connell hypothesis. It is best measured with Bever's interaction coefficient. Two species are grown in soil conditioned by their own kind, called home, and by the other, called away. With G for growth, Is = Gx(home) + Gy(home) − Gx(away) − Gy(away). A negative Is favors coexistence.

soil-bio-240.title: The fungal web that reaches out from ectomycorrhizas
soil-bio-240.text: Starve a host plant of phosphorus, and the fungal threads around its roots can grow tenfold. These threads are the extramatrical, or extraradical, mycelium: the mass of hyphae growing out into the soil from ectomycorrhizas, described in {{ref:soil-bio-173}}. It is the fungus's main body: it gathers phosphorus and other minerals, makes enzymes, colonizes new root tips and feeds invertebrates. Some hyphae branch finely to explore the soil. Others aggregate into rhizomorphs, durable water-repellent cords that carry materials like xylem. Ectomycorrhizas are small, so these hyphae greatly enlarge the surface touching soil, reaching water and nutrients that roots cannot. Lab studies predict about 23% of plant carbon goes to this mycelium, with 15-30% of that lost to respiration. In some forest soils it may hold a third of the mass of soil microbes and half the dissolved organic carbon. Its lifespan, from a few months to several years, is estimated with ergosterol or PLFA analysis, 14C dating or sand-filled ingrowth bags.

soil-bio-247.title: The mycorrhizosphere, where roots, fungi and microbes meet
soil-bio-247.text: Fungal hyphae are thinner than roots, so they reach moisture and nutrients that roots cannot. The mycorrhizosphere is the zone they help build: roots, the hyphae of their {{ref:soil-bio-157}} fungi, associated microorganisms and the soil under their direct influence. Here roots release nutrients, and the fungus raises microbial numbers and activity. Its bacteria affect nutrient uptake, protect against pathogens and help capture nitrogen from the air and weather minerals. The fungi guard against pathogens too. Glomus intraradices reduces germination of Fusarium oxysporum but stimulates the harmless Trichoderma harzianum. The fungal partner even sets protozoan numbers. A Paxillus involutus mycorrhiza lowers protozoan density, whereas Lactarius rufus and Suillus bovinus raise it. Nematodes, mites and earthworms forage on its roots, hyphae and microbes.

soil-bio-246.title: Mycorrhiza helper bacteria, the third partner underground
soil-bio-246.text: A partnership between a root and a fungus often has a third member. Mycorrhiza helper bacteria associate with ectomycorrhizal and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and improve the symbiosis. They come from many phyla. Pseudomonas and Streptomyces are the most commonly reported, and Bacillus is another. They enhance fungal growth and function and nutrient uptake by fungus and plant. Some weather minerals, releasing protons and iron that lower soil pH and recycle nutrients. Phosphate-solubilizing {{ref:soil-bio-154}} build a phosphate pool that mycorrhizas draw on, helping them establish where phosphorus is limiting. Some fix nitrogen in the soil around mycorrhizas, without the root changes legumes make. In soils rich in toxic metals they help block plant uptake of lead, zinc and cadmium, which makes them candidates for cleaning up polluted soils. Most studies show them fighting pathogens with acids and antifungal metabolites and promoting plant defenses. In a few cases, though, they aided pathogenic fungi. How these interactions work is not well understood.

soil-bio-242.title: Fine roots, the working ends of a root system
soil-bio-242.text: The birth, death and decay of fine roots can account for 20-80% of net primary production in the cycling of carbon and nutrients through forests. Fine roots are usually defined as two millimeters or less in diameter. They take up and move water and nutrients, making them the root-system counterpart of leaves and twigs. They make up most of a root system's length. When they meet a nutrient patch, they lengthen, branch more and start more side roots. Their biomass and nitrogen concentration decrease with depth. They release labile carbon in exudates, feeding the soil's organic carbon directly and by stimulating microbes. Root tensile strength rises as diameter falls, so fine roots are stronger than coarse roots and help reinforce slopes against erosion. In trees, fine roots are usually colonized by a single mycorrhizal type, arbuscular or ecto.

soil-bio-244.title: Lateral roots, the branches that spread a root system
soil-bio-244.text: Two lateral roots never form directly opposite each other. A lateral root grows sideways from the primary root. It arises in the pericycle, a layer inside the root, and builds up the branching pattern of a root system. Their number matches the number of xylem bundles. Lateral roots anchor the plant, increase water uptake and nutrient extraction, and enlarge the root system's surface area. Some form symbioses with rhizobia and mycorrhizal fungi that raise nutrient uptake further. The hormone auxin, or IAA, is required at several stages of their development.

soil-bio-238.title: Bradyrhizobium, the slow grower that feeds soybeans
soil-bio-238.text: Grain legumes grown on about 1.5 million km2 a year fix about 44–66 million tons of nitrogen, almost half of the nitrogen used in agriculture. Bradyrhizobium is a genus of Gram-negative soil bacteria, many of which fix nitrogen in legume root nodules. They are slow-growing rhizobia, taking 3–5 days to cloud a liquid medium, unlike the fast-growing {{ref:soil-bio-239}}. Bradyrhizobium japonicum nodulates soybeans, cowpeas and mung beans, and commercial inoculants are available. The genus is also a major member of forest soil microbial communities, where its strains usually cannot fix nitrogen or form nodules.

soil-bio-252.title: Rhizotrons, laboratories built underground
soil-bio-252.text: Some laboratories are built below ground. A rhizotron is an underground laboratory for studying soil and its interactions with plants and animals. A central corridor usually has viewing windows into the soil profiles on either side. Separate outside bays allow experiments that vary the soil composition and the plants and animals in it. Rhizotrons operate at Kew Gardens, at a USDA research station in Houghton, Michigan, at Treborth Botanic Garden in Wales and at Charles Sturt University in Australia.

soil-bio-237.title: Azospirillum, a root partner sold by the million
soil-bio-237.text: Over 113 plant species in 35 families have benefited from Azospirillum. These Gram-negative bacteria prefer low oxygen, fix nitrogen and can promote plant growth. They live in soil and fresh water, especially close to roots. Many excrete plant hormones that make roots grow more branches and fine root hairs, and they make nitrogen and phosphorus more available. They curb disease by competing with pathogens for space and iron. How much nitrogen they supply by fixation is still debated. In the 1970s Johanna Döbereiner's group in Brazil found root-associated strains that fix nitrogen. Commercial inoculants appeared in 2009 and exceeded 3 million doses a year by 2018.

soil-bio-241.title: Exploration types: sorting fungi by how far they reach
soil-bio-241.text: In 2001 Agerer proposed sorting ectomycorrhizal fungi into exploration types. The scheme classes them by the growth pattern and biomass of their extramatrical mycelium and whether they form rhizomorphs. Four types are commonly recognized: contact, short-distance, medium-distance and long-distance. Long-distance types form rhizomorphs with hollow, vessel-like tubes, take up more organic nitrogen and are thought less competitive in disturbed systems. In pine systems they dominate where roots are sparse. Short-distance types, cheaper in carbon, dominate where roots are dense. Many fungi fall along a gradient rather than into one type. The DEEMY database compiles exploration types for over 550 species.

soil-bio-248.title: How farming feeds or starves the mycorrhizosphere
soil-bio-248.text: Fungal hyphae secrete {{ref:soil-bio-121}}, an adhesive that builds stable soil aggregates and resists erosion. It accounts for about 5% of global organic carbon and nitrogen storage. How a farm is run decides whether the mycorrhizosphere that crops rely on for nutrients and pathogen resistance thrives. Growing crops side by side, as in {{ref:soil-agri-133}}, raises arbuscular mycorrhizal colonization. So do {{ref:soil-agri-098}} and less herbicide and fertilizer. Growing one crop alone, {{ref:soil-agri-053}}, weakens the symbiosis. So does frequent plowing, which severs hyphal networks, and so do fertilizers that make plants less reliant on the fungi. Mesoamerican milpa farming limits plowing and fertilizer, and maize grown with beans yields more through their shared mycorrhizosphere.

soil-bio-243.title: Sorting fine roots by size, rank and job
soil-bio-243.text: The traditional two-millimeter cutoff for a fine root is arbitrary. Roots under 0.5 mm are called very fine roots. Other schemes divide fine roots by position in the branching hierarchy or by function. Order-based classes follow the Horton–Strahler scheme. Unbranched distal tips are first-order, and two roots of the same order join to form the next order. As order rises, diameter, life span and secondary growth increase, while nitrogen content, mycorrhizal colonization and turnover decrease. Function-based classes separate absorptive fine roots, the low-order distal segments, from transport fine roots formed where they merge.

soil-bio-249.title: Plant-growth promoting fungi, helpers that are not mycorrhizas
soil-bio-249.text: Most of the fungi that help roots without forming mycorrhizas belong to the Ascomycota. Plant-growth promoting fungi are non-pathogenic, filamentous soil fungi that colonize roots, chiefly in the rhizosphere, and benefit plant health and development. They are the fungal counterpart of {{ref:soil-bio-155}}, and mycorrhizal fungi are not counted among them. Directly, they make auxins such as IAA that shape root architecture, solubilize phosphorus with organic acids and capture iron with siderophores. Indirectly, they suppress harmful soil microbes through antibiotics, mycoparasitism and competition, and trigger induced systemic resistance. Some Trichoderma species can remediate heavy metals, organometallic compounds and agrochemicals.
